title: Rebekah Says, I Will Go
hook: matchmaking is common in traditional communities
carry: a match is offered; the yes is theirs

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was confirmed: a second yes, chosen once you know more. Today a new stretch of the life cycle begins, before a couple has even met.

A Roman noblewoman, the midrash says, once put a sharp question to Rabbi Yose. If your God finished making the world, what has he been doing since? Matching couples, said Rabbi Yose. She laughed. She could do that herself; she had plenty of servants. In a single night she paired them all off. By morning they came to her bruised and complaining, each one wanting out. She went back to Rabbi Yose and admitted it. He told her that to God, joining two people is as hard as splitting the sea.
screen: `WHAT HAS GOD DONE SINCE?` → `MATCHING COUPLES.` → `ONE NIGHT, AND A BAD MORNING.`

segments.voice: You met Abraham's servant at the well back in your first year. Today, what he was doing there has a name. A shidduch is a suggested pairing, and the person who suggests it is a shadchan, a matchmaker. In traditional communities a match often begins this way: a shadchan, a teacher, a family friend says, I know someone. The two families ask questions. The two people meet. The Torah has its own matchmaking story. Abraham sends his servant to his homeland to find a wife for Isaac. At the well the servant asks God for a sign. Not beauty, not wealth: the young woman who, when he asks for a drink, gives it and offers to water his camels too. Before he has finished speaking, Rebekah comes out and does exactly that. He was looking for kindness that does more than it's asked. But a match is a suggestion, not an order. When the servant wants to leave with Rebekah, her family says they will call her and ask her. Her answer, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, is short: "I will go." Jewish law insists that a marriage needs both people's consent, and the rabbis read this moment as part of that teaching. Which brings us back to the noblewoman. She treated matching as sorting, done by morning. Rabbi Yose's answer says the opposite: a good match takes patience, knowledge of both people, and humility. The matchmaker only opens a door. The two people walk through it, or don't.
screen: `A MATCHMAKER SAYS: I KNOW SOMEONE.` · `A SIGN AT THE WELL: KINDNESS.` · `REBEKAH IS ASKED, AND ANSWERS.` · `NOT SORTING, BUT CARE.` · then, large: `REBEKAH SAYS, I WILL GO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind two people you know who don't know each other but should, and not only for romance: two new parents, two people who love the same odd hobby, a newcomer and a neighbor. Notice what each might bring the other, and how you'd make the introduction and then leave the next step to them, the way Rebekah's family left the answer to her.
Shidduch: a match. An introduction made with care by someone who knows both sides, and a yes that belongs to the two people. Today's word.
Your line: a match is offered; the yes is theirs. Rebekah was asked, and she answered. That's today, done.

howItsDone: In many traditional Jewish communities, a match is suggested by a matchmaker (shadchan), a teacher or a family friend; the families make inquiries, the two people meet, and the couple decides whether to go forward.
